opus-5.5.text:
I'd describe it as a field that existed long before the term "embodied AI" became popular. Robot grasping and manipulation was originally its own discipline, rooted in robotics, mechanics, and control. People studied grasp stability, force closure, contact models, and motion planning. A lot of that work was analytical: you had a precise model of the object and the gripper, and you computed a grasp that was physically guaranteed to hold.

Around the mid-2010s, things began to shift. Deep learning arrived, and people started asking whether a robot could learn to grasp directly from visual input instead of relying on a perfect geometric model. That opened the door to data-driven grasping: large-scale grasp datasets, learned grasp detectors, and eventually methods that generalize to objects the robot has never seen. My own group spent a lot of time there, on dexterous grasping, generalizable grasping across categories, and simulation-generated synthetic data at scale.

When "embodied AI" emerged as a broader banner, it absorbed these threads. The motivation was that intelligence shouldn't live only in text or images; it needs a body that perceives, acts, and changes the physical world. Grasping is the most basic form of that interaction. If you can't pick something up reliably, you can't do anything downstream: you can't tidy a table, you can't use tools, you can't serve anyone in a home or a factory.

So in my view, grasping and control research went from being a niche robotics problem to being the foundational layer of embodied intelligence. Traditional robotics contributed rigor in physics and control. Computer vision and machine learning contributed perception and generalization. Embodied AI is where those two communities finally merged. The big question now is how to build a general-purpose capability on top of that layer, something closer to a foundation model for action, rather than solving each task one at a time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visual input in learned grasping, but does not identify proprioceptive state as the usual input to robot-control research.

r002.rationale: It describes analytical grasping and control, but does not characterize the research as lacking closed-loop feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say that line of work has a very clear lineage, and it's worth separating it into a few stages, because the research itself changed character along the way.

The first stage, roughly the 2010s, was what I'd call classical grasping and manipulation. It came out of robotics proper, not out of AI. You had analytic approaches: model the object geometry, compute force closure, plan a grasp, execute it with a controller. That work was rigorous but brittle. Everything depended on knowing the object precisely, and in the real world you almost never do.

Then deep learning arrived, and the second stage was essentially "perception meets grasping." Work like DexNet, and later the stream of 6-DoF grasp detection methods, basically treated grasping as a vision problem. Give me a point cloud, I'll predict where to grasp. Our own work in that period, including GraspNet, was very much in this spirit: build a large dataset, define a benchmark, learn a network that generalizes across objects. The key shift was that we stopped needing a perfect object model. We just needed enough data to learn a mapping from what the camera sees to a stable grasp.

But notice what that stage still was: it was mostly open-loop. Perceive, predict, execute. The robot didn't really react to what happened after it started moving. And it was almost entirely two-finger parallel grippers, because that's what made the problem tractable.

The third stage is where I think the word "embodied" starts to become appropriate. A few things converged. One, we moved to dexterous hands and whole-body control, where the action space is high-dimensional and you can't hand-design the controller anymore. Two, simulation got good enough and fast enough that reinforcement learning became practical, and sim-to-real stopped being a fantasy. Three, and this is the big one, large pretrained models from vision and language came in and changed what "generalization" meant. Suddenly the question wasn't "can you grasp a new mug" but "can you understand an instruction, perceive an unstructured scene, and act in a closed loop over a long horizon."

So when people say grasping research "became incorporated into embodied AI," I'd characterize it this way: grasping and low-level control became the grounding layer. The reason embodied AI is hard, and the reason it's not just a language model with a body attached, is that the physics doesn't forgive you. A VLA model can describe what to do, but the contact-rich part, actually closing your fingers around something without crushing it or dropping it, is where all the earlier manipulation research still lives. It got absorbed, but it didn't become irrelevant. If anything, the bottleneck shifted onto it.

And I'd add one honest caveat. A lot of what we learned in the grasping era, about data scale, about benchmarks, about the sim-to-real gap, didn't transfer cleanly. Grasp detection could be solved with a few hundred thousand annotated scenes. General manipulation needs something closer to the data regime of language models, and we don't have an internet of robot experience. So the integration is real, but it's incomplete, and figuring out where the data comes from is, to me, the defining problem of this current stage.

r001.rationale: The response describes grasping as mapping camera input or point clouds to predicted grasps, but does not identify proprioceptive state as the usual input to robot-control research.

r002.rationale: It explicitly characterizes that stage as mostly open-loop and says the robot did not react to what happened after it started moving.

astra-6.text:
I would characterize it as an important foundation for embodied AI. Robot control and grasping already involve the central challenge: connecting perception to action in the physical world. A robot has to understand what is in front of it, decide how to interact with it, and adjust when the result differs from what it expected.

Grasping is a good example. Recognizing an object doesn’t automatically tell you how to pick it up. You have to account for its geometry, the available contact points, and what happens as you apply force. So this research was never simply about visual recognition; it was about making perception useful for action.

Embodied AI puts those capabilities into a broader framework, where an agent can combine skills to carry out longer tasks. I see that as continuity with robotics, with a growing emphasis on learning and generalization.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception and action but does not identify proprioceptive state as the usual input to robot-control research.

r002.rationale: The response says a robot adjusts when the result differs from expectations, which describes feedback rather than a lack of closed-loop feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
I would characterize it as an important foundation for embodied AI. Robotics has long studied how an agent perceives the physical world and acts on it. Grasping makes that connection very concrete: recognizing an object is only the beginning. The robot has to decide where to make contact, move its arm and fingers, and adjust as the object moves or slips.

What embodied AI adds is a broader emphasis on learning and generalization. Instead of designing a controller for one object in one carefully arranged setting, we want systems that can handle unfamiliar objects, different environments, and varied instructions. But the underlying challenges—geometry, contact, uncertainty, and feedback—are still robotics problems. So I see it as a continuation and expansion of that research.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception, geometry, contact, and uncertainty, but does not identify proprioceptive state as the usual input or contrast it with vision.

r002.rationale: The response describes adjusting as objects move or slip and names feedback as an underlying challenge; it does not characterize the research as lacking closed-loop feedback.
